column1:
Incorporating Beige Book insights alongside the April 29, 2020 FOMC statement and SLOOS strengthens the negative tone:

- Demand and activity: Reports of consumer spending weakness affecting auto dealers and general retailers, and tourism-related employment softness, align with the FOMC’s description of “sharp declines in economic activity” and “surge in job losses.”
- Manufacturing and trade: Ongoing trade-related uncertainty weighing on manufacturing reinforces downside risks to output and capex.
- Credit conditions: SLOOS’ broad-based tightening of C&I and CRE loan standards and wider spreads underscores the FOMC’s concern that the flow of credit to households and businesses is “impaired,” despite QE in Treasuries/agency MBS/CMBS and large-scale repo operations.
- Prices and inflation: While input cost influences (freight, metals, tariffs, wages, natural gas) are noted, weak demand keeps overall inflation pressures muted, consistent with the FOMC’s assessment.
- Labor markets: Even with isolated mentions of skilled labor shortages in select occupations, the dominant Beige Book themes are job losses and sectoral stress, supporting the Committee’s emphasis on “considerable risks” to employment.

Net effect: Beige Book details corroborate the deterioration in demand and credit intermediation flagged by SLOOS, with only limited offset from isolated supply-side tightness. This warrants a slightly more negative read than the SLOOS-only assessment.
